data.source_title: Workflow interruptions and stress at work: a mixed-methods study among physicians and nurses of a multidisciplinary emergency department
data.locator: Methods (Design/Setting/Sample and procedure; operational definition); Results, Figures 1-2; Discussion
data.source_setting: Emergency department of a major metropolitan academic community hospital in Augsburg, Germany
data.source_period: Published December 2017; observations on 20 randomly selected days; exact dates not stated
data.source_n: 77 matched observation/self-rating sessions; 116 hours 51 minutes observed; 877 interruptions; 791 interruptions with classified content
data.unit: interruptions per observed hour (877/116 h 51 min; paper reports 7.51/hour)
data.source_evidence_basis: Trained observers shadowed ED nurses and physicians during 90-minute sessions. Interruption defined as an unexpected task or communication causing discontinuation of the focal task and observable task switch. Common contents among 791 categorized events: parallel cases 240, current case 151, coordination 144. Parallel-case interruption events were associated with higher self-reported work stress; most interruption types showed no association.
data.limitations: One German academic ED, selected 90-minute observations, mixed-methods observational design; 80 sessions were scheduled but 77 matched. Rate depends on the paper's operational definition and denominator and must not be generalized as ED prevalence or a US/RWJUH estimate. Association does not establish causation or harm.
data.inferred_scenario_use: Optional synthetic interruption about a parallel patient or coordination can test task resumption and rechecking. Keep event timing and frequency authored as synthetic, not calibrated to the observed rate.
